name: SMV tier-list threads

card.summary: Forum threads that sort physiques, facial features, surgeries or traits into ranked tiers, giving members a quick map of which improvements are widely thought to change perceived attractiveness the most.
card.aka: muscle SMV tier list, looks tier list
card.note: Tier lists are subjective community rankings, not measurements.

quick.overview:
SMV tier-list threads are posts on looksmaxxing forums in which a member ranks items (muscle groups, facial features, procedures, supplements, even ethnic groups) into S/A/B-style tiers. SMV stands for sexual market value, the community's term for overall attractiveness.

For appearance improvement, the lists work as a prioritisation shorthand: a member who sees height and frame near the top of a features list, or a particular surgery rated highly, can decide where to put effort. They are opinion posts, usually followed by replies disputing the placements; the format itself comes from video-game culture.
quick.how: Members post a list with tier headings, others reply with their own rankings or objections, and popular threads get updated versions. Topics range from muscle SMV and dimorphic features to surgeries, SARMs and anime. Readers use them as a starting point for further research rather than as measurements.
quick.risks: Lists are subjective and often disagree with each other. Some rank medical procedures or performance-enhancing compounds, and the placements reflect the poster's opinion, not clinical guidance. Some threads rank groups of people, which is contentious even within the community.

lead: SMV tier-list threads are forum posts, mainly on looksmax.org, that rank things related to attractiveness into labelled tiers. 'SMV' stands for sexual market value, a term that began on pick-up-artist forums and later spread through the wider manosphere and incel-adjacent spaces, where people are rated on a 1-to-10 decile scale or a 1-to-8 'PSL' scale [1].

The tier-list format began in video-game communities, where players sorted characters and in-game elements by tournament viability; the top 'S' grade echoes Japanese academic and advertising grading [2][11]. Looksmaxxing forums borrowed the layout to sort anything from muscle groups and facial features to cosmetic surgeries and supplements.

For someone trying to look better, these lists serve as a prioritisation map. A 'Tier List of Dimorphic Features (Men)' thread, for example, put height and frame in the top tier, jaw and neck width next, and facial hair and hairline shape in a bottom tier, while replies debated whether height counts as dimorphic [3]. Other threads rank plastic and cosmetic surgeries, SARMs, muscle groups and body features [4][5][6]. Published attractiveness research looks at individual traits and their combinations, for instance height and shoulder-to-hip ratio together, rather than at forum rankings [12]; the tier lists themselves record community opinion.

chain: Members rank features, muscles or procedures into tiers
Readers see which items the community thinks matter most
They choose where to spend effort on their own appearance
angle.text: The lists condense community opinion into a quick ordering of what to work on, such as muscle groups, frame, or surgeries. They are used as a starting point for deciding priorities, with the ranking itself coming from forum consensus and argument.

infobox: Muscle SMV, dimorphic features, surgeries, SARMs

paras: A tier list sorts items into ordered groups, typically S, A, B, C and D, from most to least favourable. The format grew out of video-game culture, where players ranked playable characters in fighting games such as Tekken and Super Smash Bros., and in games like League of Legends and Overwatch, by how viable they were in competitive play [11]. It later spread to films, sports teams, logos, animals and many other subjects, usually to prompt discussion or give a quick overview [2][11].

On looksmaxxing forums the same layout is applied to appearance. Examples include threads titled 'muscle SMV tier list', 'plastic surgery tier list', 'softmax tier list', 'updated roidmaxxing tier list for bone mass and masculinization' and a thread tier-listing SARMs with suggested stacks [4][6][7][10]. Some threads rank by race or by country, and others are jokes such as looksmaxxing theme songs, anime or hardest punchers [8]. Threads that rank groups of people are contentious and are not described here beyond noting that they exist.

Sexual market value is described as the manosphere's counterpart to the academic idea of erotic capital, which British sociologist Catherine Hakim introduced in the early 2000s and set out in a 2010 article and a 2011 book. Hakim presented erotic capital as a fourth personal asset alongside economic, cultural and social capital, made up of beauty, sexual attractiveness, social attractiveness, vivaciousness, social presentation and sexuality [1][13].

Within manosphere forums, people are placed on decile or PSL scales, with high scorers labelled 'Chad' and low scorers 'sub-5' or 'incel'. Raters often combine looks, money and status into one overall score [1]. A tier list is a coarser version of this scoring: instead of numbering a person, it grades an attribute or an intervention.

sections.h: Origins and spread of the format
paras: The Wikipedia entry on tier lists does not date the format's first appearance, but notes that fighting-game communities were its main home. Guilty Gear Xrd rosters were sorted into S, S-, A+ and A tiers (covered by Red Bull in 2016), Smashboards produced annual polled Super Smash Bros. lists, and outlets such as Kotaku, The Daily Dot and PC Gamer published their own [11]. Around 2020 a related 'iceberg chart' variant became popular, ranking items by how widely known they are [11].

Looksmaxxing members adopted the template because it compresses a long debate into one image or post. Popular lists are updated and re-posted in new versions, and replies often become the real content as other members argue over placements or post alternatives [3][9].

One thread on male dimorphic features listed height and frame in tier 1, jaw and neck width in tier 2, chin height and browridge projection in tier 3, occipital shape and nose slope in tier 4, and facial hair and hairline shape in a lowest tier. A reply questioned whether height is dimorphic, and another answered that it is [3].

A 'muscle SMV' thread ranks which muscle groups are thought to contribute most to perceived attractiveness, and a roidmaxxing list ranks anabolic compounds by their assumed effect on bone mass and masculinisation [4][7]. These are posters' opinions; the compound list in particular describes illicit or prescription-only drugs and is not guidance.

A surgery tier list graded procedures from acceptable to disliked, with the poster giving reasons for each placement; replies mostly tagged other members [9]. A plastic-surgery list and a 'softmax' list (non-surgical improvements) work similarly [5][6]. A SARMs thread ranked compounds by potency and selectivity and added example stacks, with the author asking readers to correct mistakes [10]. These reflect personal opinion and experience, not clinical recommendation.

No studies of looksmaxxing tier lists as such have been published. Researchers describing SMV note that it parallels the sociological concept of erotic capital, and that concept has drawn criticism: that it falls more heavily on women although presented as universal, that female sexuality varies more across cultures and classes, that it overstates how far individuals can change their own capital, and, in Adam Isaiah Green's 'sexual fields' view, that attractiveness depends on the particular social field rather than being a portable asset [1][13].

Experimental attractiveness research examines traits in combination. In four studies with 659 heterosexual women recruited online, Pazhoohi, Garza and Kingstone found that taller male figures and figures with broader shoulder-to-hip ratios were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable fighters, and that broader shoulders raised ratings for taller figures but not shorter ones in the final study using realistic renderings. The authors describe the work as preliminary, and the stimuli were computer-generated figures [12]. The finding that traits interact is one reason forum members argue about rankings that treat features in isolation.

On the format itself, games journalist Maddy Myers of Kotaku argued that tier lists work poorly for team-based games because roles and composition add variables, and that a game's tier list can shift after updates or as players refine techniques [11].

Tier-list threads are a common way for newer members to orient themselves. The replies often become the real content, with members disputing placements or posting their own versions, and the format is also used humorously [8]. Because the lists cover both free habits and costly or risky procedures on the same scale, readers use them as a starting point for further reading rather than as instructions [6][9].

timeline.event: Catherine Hakim introduces the term 'erotic capital', the academic counterpart later compared to SMV [1][13].
Hakim publishes her formal account of erotic capital in the European Sociological Review; a book follows in 2011 [1][13].
Smashboards publishes a polled Super Smash Bros. Melee tier list covered by The Daily Dot, an example of the video-game format [11].
Red Bull covers Guilty Gear Xrd tier rankings; Kotaku and The Daily Dot publish Overwatch tier lists [11].
Looksmax.org threads such as 'muscle smv tier list' and 'Tier list for surgeries' circulate [4][9].
Further looksmax.org lists appear, including dimorphic features, plastic surgery and softmax [3][5][6].

lore.intro: Members use tier lists as shared shorthand for what matters in appearance, while regularly disputing individual placements [3][9].

claims.claim: Height and frame sit at the top of male features
claims.believers: A poster ranked height and frame in the highest tier of male dimorphic features, ahead of jaw and neck width [3].
claims.experts: Experimental work by Pazhoohi and colleagues found taller figures with broader shoulder-to-hip ratios rated more attractive by women, with an interaction between the two; the sample was online and the stimuli computer-generated [12]. No study has tested the forum's full ordering.

claims.claim: Muscle can be ranked by SMV impact
claims.believers: Muscle SMV tier-list threads rank which muscle groups contribute most to perceived attractiveness [4].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined a muscle-group ranking of this kind; shoulder-to-hip ratio is the closest studied trait [12].

claims.claim: Surgeries can be graded into tiers
claims.believers: A surgery thread grades procedures from acceptable to disliked with reasons given for each placement [9][6].
claims.experts: No published study validates a community tier ranking of procedures; clinical outcomes are assessed procedure by procedure.

claims.claim: Attractiveness is a market value that can be scored
claims.believers: SMV users rate people on 1-to-10 or PSL scales and sometimes combine looks, money and status [1].
claims.experts: Sociologists treat the related idea of erotic capital as contested: Green argues its value depends on the sexual field, and others say it overstates individual control [1][13].

claims.claim: A ranking can guide which improvements to prioritise
claims.believers: Members use lists as a starting point to decide where to put effort [3][4].
claims.experts: Games journalist Maddy Myers notes tier lists flatten context and can shift as conditions change [11].
